> list the apps you can use and the 3 i should connect next.

> at 9pm, flag conflicts and write prep notes for tomorrow's meetings.

> 5 lines a day on my topics, with sources. stay quiet on slow days.

> watch my watchlist and write one research idea a week with the risks. research only. no trades.

> draft in my voice from brandDNA.md, find outlier posts by bookmarks and replies per view, and score yesterday's posts.

> when i ask for code, hand it to a cloud agent, open a PR, never merge, and have a reviewer bot grade it.

> package the bots that work as shareable templates. strip anything personal.

→ one chief of staff, not 98 loose bots

→ dashboards over notifications

which room would you build first?

I don't think prompt-injection filtering can be a security boundary for agents on its own. OWASP maps nine dimensions of prompt injection, and a filter tuned for one misses the others, so enforcement has to sit at the action layer.

For each agent-to-tool integration, decide which layers you rely on: input filtering, a logged runtime check per action (allow, ask or block against a declared policy), and a sandbox that limits the damage if the model gets it wrong.

For an agent with database access, reads are allowed, writes need human approval, schema changes and exports are blocked, and everything runs in an isolated sandbox with scoped credentials. If you can only name the first layer, I think that is your real answer.

▲ Anthropic just shipped Code Mode in Claude Code, so Claude can now write JavaScript that chains its own tool calls in 1 step.

The key idea is simple. Without Code Mode, Claude asks for each Bash, Read or Edit call and reads every result. With Code Mode, Claude writes 1 program that runs commands in parallel, feeds one result into the next call, and returns only the output it needs.

The numbers: code that runs in the background can keep going for up to 2 hours while you keep talking to Claude. Anthropic's related code execution with MCP pattern cut 1 workflow from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens. It is a trade-off though: Anthropic publishes no token figure for Code Mode itself, code Claude waits on stops after 10 minutes, and auto mode reviews the code, not each tool call.

It is experimental and off by default. Opt in with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 on Claude Code v2.1.323 or later. It works with Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.2, in the terminal, on the Anthropic API only......

THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

the full tree
> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted
> JEV routes micro-forks in milliseconds

paste the tree and this prompt into Claude Code ↓

2. Create three read-only Haiku 5.5 subagents: search (maps the repo), grep (finds call sites), docs (pulls the API reference).
3. Add one rule to CLAUDE.md: consult the advisor before locking a plan, after the same error twice, and before calling a task done.
4. Route fast deterministic forks (tool choice, path selection, retries) through JEV.
Show me every change as a diff first. No edits until I say go."

I don't think prompt-injection filtering can be a security boundary for agents on its own. OWASP maps nine dimensions of prompt injection, and a filter tuned for one misses the others, so enforcement has to sit at the action layer.

For each agent-to-tool integration, decide which layers you rely on: input filtering, a logged runtime check per action (allow, ask or block against a declared policy), and a sandbox that limits the damage if the model gets it wrong.

For an agent with database access, reads are allowed, writes need human approval, schema changes and exports are blocked, and everything runs in an isolated sandbox with scoped credentials. If you can only name the first layer, I think that is your real answer.

outsiders.text:
▲ Anthropic just shipped Code Mode in Claude Code, so Claude can now write JavaScript that chains its own tool calls in 1 step.

The key idea is simple. Without Code Mode, Claude asks for each Bash, Read or Edit call and reads every result. With Code Mode, Claude writes 1 program that runs commands in parallel, feeds one result into the next call, and returns only the output it needs.

The numbers: code that runs in the background can keep going for up to 2 hours while you keep talking to Claude. Anthropic's related code execution with MCP pattern cut 1 workflow from 150,000 to 2,000 tokens. It is a trade-off though: Anthropic publishes no token figure for Code Mode itself, code Claude waits on stops after 10 minutes, and auto mode reviews the code, not each tool call.

It is experimental and off by default. Opt in with CLAUDE_CODE_EXPERIMENTAL_CODE_MODE=1 on Claude Code v2.1.323 or later. It works with Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, Haiku 5.5 and Fable 5.2, in the terminal, on the Anthropic API only......

THIS IS ACTUAL F*CKING GOLD

Anthropic just shared one of the best tricks for Claude Code.

The idea: run Sonnet, Haiku and Opus 5.5 together, each one doing only the job it's best at.

Opus-level judgment on every big call, without paying Opus rates for every routine turn.

You just launch Claude Code like this:

claude --model sonnet --advisor opus

here's the split:

→ Sonnet 5.5 runs the session and writes the code
→ Haiku 5.5 explores files and docs in parallel
→ Opus 5.5 stays on call as advisor for the big calls
→ you stop spending Opus on work that doesn't need it

Opus only steps in at three moments:

→ before a plan locks
→ when the same error shows up twice
→ before calling it done

Sonnet builds. Haiku explores. Opus reviews.

JEV engineering is the same move one layer down: the forks that need no thinker (which file, which tool, retry or stop) go to JEV in milliseconds, and the big models only see the ones that split

> Sonnet 5.5 runs the main session and edits code
> search maps the repo on Haiku 5.5
> grep finds call sites on Haiku 5.5
> docs pulls the API reference on Haiku 5.5
> Opus 5.5 on call as advisor, reads the whole transcript when consulted
